name: abstract-document
intent: Represent a hierarchical object as one loosely typed property map plus child documents, then project narrow typed view interfaces over that shared state. It lets independently deployed concerns add runtime properties while callers of known properties retain discoverable access, explicit ownership and boundary validation.
problem: In a statically typed model, the complete property set may be unknown until runtime — plugin- or tenant-specific fields, evolving configuration, JSON or document-store trees, and user-defined UI data. Fixed classes force schema changes and combinatorial variants; exposing Map<String, Object> everywhere loses ownership, discoverability and type checks. The problem is to keep one extensible tree without letting its untyped representation become the domain API.
context: Applies where the data genuinely is dynamic and the code that consumes it is statically typed. Typical settings are extensible domain models whose features live in separate modules, documents arriving from serialisation or a document-oriented store, and framework/tooling code that traverses properties generically. It is a model or boundary representation, not a replacement for typed values in hot inner loops.
benefits: New properties can be introduced by the subsystem that needs them, without editing a shared class, a base type or a database schema — the extension point is a key, not a field.
Call sites that know a property keep type-safe, discoverable access through a small view interface, so the untyped representation stays mostly inside the model layer.

One uniform representation for a whole tree: nested documents, serialisation and generic traversal (get/put/children) work the same at every level, and ordinary map or JSON libraries can read and write it.
Views compose instead of inheriting: a noun type is the union of the views it implements, so capabilities can be mixed per object without a deep or duplicated hierarchy.
Different consumers can see the same data through different views — a pricing view, an inventory view, a presentation view — each owning its keys and casting only what it needs.
Schema evolution is additive by construction: unknown properties are preserved rather than rejected, which suits document-oriented stores and plugin extensibility.
Serialisation is uniform and trivial: the entire object tree is one map structure, so any JSON/YAML library can round-trip it without custom binding code.
Subsystems can ship new views independently: a plugin can add its own view interface over the same document without coordinating with the host or other plugins.
tradeoffs: The contract is not compiler-checked: a value stored under the wrong type fails at the accessor cast rather than at the write, and a mistyped key silently yields an empty view.
String keys are a weak contract — no rename safety, no discoverability, no exhaustiveness; key constants and required-property checks must be maintained by hand.
Aliasing: every view reads and writes the same mutable map, so one subsystem can change another's data, while making the document immutable turns all views read-only.
Each property costs a map entry, a boxed value and a cast per read, so memory use and indirection are worse than typed fields for large object counts or tight loops.
Tooling sees a map instead of fields: bean-oriented frameworks, object-relational mappers, debuggers and schema generators need adapters or lose their information.
Validation is deferred: without a checking factory the document is validated only when some view happens to read a property, so failures surface deep in the call chain.
Debugging is harder: watch variables show a map of string keys rather than named fields, and stack traces reference the generic document interface rather than the business-logical accessor.
Key collisions between subsystems produce silent data corruption: two independent plugins that happen to use the same string key will overwrite each other's values with no warning.

participants.responsibility: Map-like contract over a document — put(key, value), get(key) and children(key, constructor) — that says nothing about which keys exist.
Implements that contract over a single property map plus child documents, finalises the generic accessors and rebuilds typed child views from the raw maps.
One narrow interface per concern (HasModel, HasPrice, HasParts) whose accessors read and cast the keys that concern owns; this is the type callers see, not the storage type.
Stable key (constant or enum member) identifying a property; shared by writers and views and the only thing tying the two together.
Union of view interfaces built on the base document; holds no state of its own beyond the shared document, so several views can be composed over one object.
Programs against views for the properties it knows and against the document contract for generic traversal, persistence or extension data.

use_cases: Extensible domain models where a host system defines the core model and plugins add their own properties and views without touching the core classes.
Configuration and settings trees loaded from JSON/YAML and exposed to each subsystem as a typed view of only the keys that subsystem owns.
Documents from a document-oriented store or a message payload whose fields vary per tenant or version, presented to typed code as views over the same underlying document.
Framework and tooling code — editors, dynamic forms, rule engines, report builders — that enumerates and manipulates properties generically while using views for the values it understands.
Data-driven user interfaces: the pattern's original setting, where components are configured at runtime and their fields are addressed by key and read through typed getters.
Interchange layers where one document must serve several consumers that care about different, overlapping subsets of its properties.

Content Management Systems (CMS) where articles, images, videos and other content types share common attributes (creation date, author, tags) but have type-specific attributes (image dimensions, video duration).
E-commerce platforms where product types (physical goods, digital downloads, subscriptions) share name/price/description but differ on shipping weight, download links, or billing intervals.

Library management systems handling books in multiple formats (physical, eBook, audiobook) where each format has distinct attributes (page count, file size, duration) but shared bibliographic metadata.
Medical records systems where patient demographics, history, test results and prescriptions share a patient ID but otherwise have specialised, evolving schemas.
Project management tools where tasks, milestones and issues share name/assignee but need type-specific fields (milestone date, issue priority, time tracking).
Educational platforms with diverse learning materials (text, video, quiz, assignment) sharing title/author/date but needing duration, due date or score fields.
Software build systems and plugin architectures where third-party extensions contribute configuration keys unknown to the host application.
Speedment's Java metadata tooling, cited by the pattern's originator as a real-world implementation of Abstract Document for database metadata.
Jackson databind's JsonNode/ObjectNode tree model, where a JSON tree can be inspected dynamically and selected subtrees converted to typed views.
System.Text.Json's JsonNode/JsonObject DOM, intended for JSON payloads with no fixed schema that must be inspected before typed deserialization.
avoid_when: The property set is known and stable: use real fields on classes, records or structs and let the compiler check them.
The only reason for the map is serialisation: bind a plain data class with Jackson, Gson, serde, Codable or encoding/json at the boundary instead of making the map the in-memory model.

The document crosses a boundary and no downstream code needs unknown fields: validate and convert it into typed objects at the boundary, keeping the map local rather than letting it spread through the domain.

It is a hot path: many small objects or frequent reads make boxed map entries, hashing and per-read casts cost more than indexed fields; prefer typed fields, value types or a Flyweight where appropriate.
Full encapsulation or immutable value semantics are required: value objects and records with defensive copies express those better.

The implementation language is already dynamic and no static view layer is wanted: plain dicts, hashes or objects plus local conventions are the simpler equivalent — this pattern exists to buy type-safe views back.
All consumers are co-located and agree on the schema: shared typed classes with no runtime variation are simpler and safer.
anti_patterns: "Stringly typed" domain code: the property map spreads out of the model layer, so business logic reads and writes raw keys and the compiler checks nothing; unlike Abstract Document, the untyped representation has become the domain API.

Publishing get(key)/put(key, value) to every caller leaves no view owning a key, so each call site casts for itself; Abstract Document instead keeps these operations behind a document boundary and typed views.
Handing one mutable map to many components that each believe they own it produces action-at-a-distance bugs; the pattern's shared document is safe only with explicit ownership and mutation policy.

One giant document with dozens of keys used as a substitute for a class becomes a god object without the compiler's help; Abstract Document works by composing focused views over a deliberately dynamic subset.

Storing values whose required type is validated nowhere makes the document correct only until the first reader casts it; a checking factory or typed setter is part of a usable Abstract Document implementation.

Copying view data into a fresh map makes writes to the original document invisible to the view and vice versa; Abstract Document's views must preserve the shared-document invariant or explicitly be immutable snapshots.
design_principles: Interface segregation: split properties into one narrow view interface per concern so callers see only the capabilities they need.
Open/closed: new properties and views extend the model without modifying the base document or the existing noun types.
Composition over inheritance: a noun type composes its capabilities by implementing views, avoiding a combinatorial hierarchy.
Separation of concerns: the storage representation (map plus children), the access contracts (views) and the traversal mechanism (constructors) stay separate.
Information hiding: keys and casts live inside views, so callers depend on accessors rather than on the storage layout.
Data abstraction: one uniform document interface over heterogeneous data, so serialisation and traversal code is written once.
Uniform Access Principle: clients of a property should not be able to tell whether it is stored or computed — the view interface hides whether a value came from the map or is derived.
best_practices: Route every read and write through views; keep raw get/put inside the document layer and the views.
Keep keys in shared constants or an enum owned by the view that documents the property — never scatter string literals through call sites.
Validate required properties and their types when a document enters the system, with a checking factory, instead of at first read.
Decide mutability up front: either treat documents as mutable shared state with explicit ownership, or wrap the map in an unmodifiable view and accept that all views become read-only.
Rebuild child views from the raw maps through the supplied constructor so writes propagate; never hand out bare maps or cache views over stale data.
Use the pattern only where the data is genuinely dynamic and convert to typed objects at the boundary where it is not.
Track schema evolution: untyped documents outlive code, so keep a version/key registry and migrate or default missing keys explicitly.
Name key constants with a namespace prefix matching the view name to reduce the risk of accidental key collisions between independent views (e.g. HasPrice.PRICE vs HasInventory.PRICE are distinct).
Make the Document interface sealed or final where possible so that no ad-hoc implementations can bypass the view layer.
Write unit tests that verify the view accessor returns empty/throws for missing keys and correct values for present keys — the map interface cannot be tested at the compiler.
Document the expected type of each property in the view interface's Javadoc or docstring; the cast in the accessor is the only type enforcement.
When integrating with ORMs or bean frameworks, create an adapter that exposes the document's properties as named fields rather than letting the framework treat the whole map as an opaque blob.

related_patterns_notes.property-accessor: Conceptual ancestor: Fowler's 1997 Property Accessor pattern family (Flexible Dynamic Property, Defined Dynamic Property, Typed Dynamic Property, Separate Properties, Dynamic Property Knowledge Level) defines the taxonomy of dynamic property access that Abstract Document instantiates for hierarchical document trees; unlike the general family, it prescribes shared child documents plus typed views; source: https://martinfowler.com/apsupp/properties.pdf
related_patterns_notes.composite: Both patterns build tree structures of objects; the Abstract Document uses Composite's recursive composition idea for child document traversal via the children(key, constructor) method, but differs in that Composite is statically typed with fixed node interfaces while the Document is a loosely typed property map.
related_patterns_notes.extension-object: Both address the problem of adding responsibilities to an object after it is defined. Extension Object attaches new interfaces to an existing object at runtime; Abstract Document achieves the same end by composing a Document with typed view interfaces. The key distinction is that Extension Object adds new interfaces to the same object, while Abstract Document separates the storage (Document) from the interface (views).
related_patterns_notes.role-object: Both decompose an object's behaviour into composable roles or views. Role Object models each role as a separate object that the primary delegates to; Abstract Document models each concern as a view interface over a shared property map. Role Object is better when roles have behaviour; Abstract Document is better when the main concern is data with varying schema.
related_patterns_notes.metadata-mapping: Both sit between structured data and typed objects. Metadata Mapping typically maps relational rows to objects using descriptors; Abstract Document maps a property map to typed views. The metadata mapping layer often uses a dynamic property map internally when handling flexible schemas.
related_patterns_notes.document-message: Both deal with structured document-like data; Document Message packages a document as an immutable message for transmission, while Abstract Document is the in-memory representation strategy that Document Message might serialise. They compose naturally: Abstract Document is the model, Document Message is the wire format.
related_patterns_notes.layer-supertype: Layer Supertype centralises common state and behaviour through inheritance; Abstract Document's base supplies only generic document mechanics while concrete noun types compose independent typed views, so it does not require a shared domain superclass for every capability.
related_patterns_notes.user-defined-field: Fowler's UserDefinedField (Variable State) pattern — storing extra fields in a hashmap — is the lightweight ancestor of the Abstract Document's property map. The Abstract Document adds the typed view layer on top of the hashmap to recover type safety that Variable State sacrifices; source: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/UserDefinedField.html
